title: Teaching income and the shift to online lessons
summary: Most income comes from home lessons on several instruments; students stayed on online, and she now teaches seven days a week. She used to drive 50 miles a day.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Okay. So most of the time in my life I spend alone, just like I am now, in my house, preparing my lessons, cooking, practicing, and doing computer work, and that continues. Mostly every afternoon, well most of my income I should say comes from lessons: flute, sax, tenor sax, alto sax, piano, and clarinet lessons, house to house, which obviously is not an option now. I imagined at the beginning that most of my students would be running out of money and not be able to pay for online lessons because their jobs are closed, and that’s not the case at all. I completely misjudged — this is an affluent community and they were very anxious to continue lessons. It also helps them because obviously the moms are very overwhelmed right now in a way they never expected. So I would say that out of all these, like I have between 25 and 30 students, all but three families have signed on, so that’s a big load. I am teaching every day. Seven days, instead of the usual six. I try to keep the mornings for myself and the evenings for myself and that’s working out well so I start at twelve, one, finish around six, and I try to give myself breaks in between lessons. Because it’s very intense. You do need breaks. I really need to rest. It’s a lot more intense than personal, in person lessons.
Well before you were traveling to people’s homes?
Yeah. It was a good 25 miles at least every day, each way, so 50 miles a day, six days a week, and sometimes a little bit more than that. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
